title: A KING’S MOTHER WARNED HIM ABOUT WOMEN, WINE, AND JUSTICE—BUT HER GREATEST FEAR WAS WHAT POWER COULD DO TO HIS SOUL
paragraphs: A KING’S MOTHER WARNED HIM ABOUT WOMEN, WINE, AND JUSTICE—BUT HER GREATEST FEAR WAS WHAT POWER COULD DO TO HIS SOUL

Before her son could destroy a kingdom, a mother confronted three dangers that could destroy the man beneath the crown. Hidden inside Proverbs 31:1–9 is a warning about desire, addiction, forgotten people, and the kind of righteousness that points us to Jesus Christ.

Imagine being a mother who has watched her son grow from a helpless infant into a man powerful enough to command armies, pronounce judgments, and determine whether other people live in freedom or suffer under oppression.
You remember the little hands that once reached for yours.
The voice that once called for you in the middle of the night.
The child you prayed over when nobody else was watching.
And now those same hands can sign decrees that change thousands of lives.
Those same lips can speak words that either defend the innocent or condemn them.
And the boy you once carried in your arms has become a man whose private weaknesses could become an entire nation's suffering.
What would you tell him?
Would you remind him how powerful he had become?
Would you congratulate him on his throne?
Would you tell him to protect his reputation, secure his wealth, and enjoy everything his position could provide?
Not this mother.
She looked at her son and gave him something far more valuable than royal praise.
She gave him a warning.
And what makes her warning so unsettling is that she wasn't merely concerned about enemies outside the palace.
She was concerned about what could happen inside her son's heart.
Because sometimes the greatest danger to a kingdom is not an invading army.
Sometimes it is a ruler who has stopped ruling himself.
And before you dismiss this as an ancient conversation between a mother and a king, consider something uncomfortable.
You may never sit on a throne.
But you have influence over someone.
You have desires that can either be governed or allowed to govern you.
You have moments when your judgment can be clouded.
And somewhere in your world, someone vulnerable may be depending on whether you choose what is right over what is convenient.
This is why Proverbs 31 begins with a mother's warning instead of the famous description of a virtuous woman.
Before Scripture describes a woman of noble character, it records a mother teaching her son what noble leadership requires.
And the first nine verses deserve far more attention than they usually receive.
"The words of king Lemuel, the prophecy that his mother taught him." — Proverbs 31:1, KJV
The Hebrew begins:
דִּבְרֵי לְמוּאֵל מֶלֶךְ מַשָּׂא אֲשֶׁר־יִסְּרַתּוּ אִמּוֹ
Divrei Lemu'el melekh, massa asher yisserattu immo.
These are the words of King Lemuel, the weighty instruction his mother taught him.

The Hebrew word massa (מַשָּׂא) can describe an oracle or solemn pronouncement. Translators differ on how it should be understood here, and some interpret it in relation to a place called Massa. What is unmistakable is that the passage presents a mother's serious instruction to her royal son.
We are not told with certainty who Lemuel was.
Some traditions associate him with Solomon, but Scripture does not explicitly identify him as Solomon. We should not turn a possibility into a biblical fact.
Nor does the passage reveal his mother's name.
But it preserves her words.
And perhaps that is fitting.
Her identity remains largely hidden, while the truth she spoke continues to confront people thousands of years later.
Listen to how she begins.
"What, my son? and what, the son of my womb? and what, the son of my vows?" — Proverbs 31:2, KJV
There is tenderness here.
But there is urgency too.
In Hebrew, the repeated word mah (מַה), meaning "what," gives her opening an emotionally striking rhythm.
"What, my son? What, son of my womb? What, son of my vows?"
She is not simply addressing a government official.
She is addressing the child she bore.
The son connected to her deepest commitments and prayers.
She wants him to remember who he is before he forgets what he is responsible for.
Imagine hearing your mother speak like that.
Not because she hates you.
Not because she wants to control every decision you make.
But because she knows that becoming powerful does not automatically make someone wise.
And she understands something many people learn only after painful consequences.
The ability to do whatever you want is not the same as the wisdom to do what is right.
Then comes her first warning.
"Give not thy strength unto women, nor thy ways to that which destroyeth kings." — Proverbs 31:3, KJV
The Hebrew says:
אַל־תִּתֵּן לַנָּשִׁים חֵילֶךָ
Al-titten lanashim cheilek.
Literally, the opening warns against giving one's chayil—strength, capacity, or resources—to women.
But we must handle this carefully.
This is not a declaration that women are inherently dangerous.

That interpretation would contradict the wider witness of Proverbs, which celebrates wisdom through the imagery of a woman and concludes this very chapter by honoring a woman of extraordinary strength and character.
The warning concerns the destructive surrender of a ruler's strength to sexual entanglements and relationships that undermine faithful leadership.
It is about misdirected desire.
About appetites becoming masters.
About a man allowing pleasure to consume the strength he was entrusted to use responsibly.
And Scripture gives us sobering examples of what happens when desire overrules wisdom.
Consider Solomon.
First Kings 11 tells us that Solomon loved many foreign women, and that his wives turned his heart toward other gods.
The tragedy was not that Solomon had never encountered wisdom.
It was that possessing wisdom did not guarantee he would obey it.
He could speak wisely and still choose foolishly.
He could build a magnificent temple and still allow his heart to wander.
He could possess astonishing wealth and still become spiritually impoverished.
How many people are living some version of that contradiction right now?
A person who can explain biblical principles but refuses to confront a hidden addiction.
A spouse who speaks about faithfulness publicly while nurturing betrayal privately.
A ministry leader who knows how to encourage others but no longer listens when Scripture confronts personal sin.
A believer who has learned to look spiritually mature while quietly surrendering to desires that are destroying the soul.
And here is the part that hurts.
Destructive compromise rarely introduces itself as destruction.
It usually begins by promising comfort.
A little attention.
A private conversation.
A harmless indulgence.
A secret that supposedly doesn't matter.
Until one day, the thing you thought you controlled begins controlling you.
The mother's warning is not that love is dangerous.
It is that ungoverned desire can make even a powerful person dangerously weak.
And Jesus takes the issue deeper than external behavior.
In Matthew 5:27–28, He teaches that adultery is not merely an outward act; lustful intent exposes a problem within the heart.
Christ does not simply call us to avoid scandal.
He calls us to purity.
Not merely to protect appearances.
But to surrender the desires beneath them.
Because the Gospel is not a public-relations strategy for hiding sin.
It is God's invitation to bring sin into the light and be transformed by grace.
But the mother is not finished.
She turns from sexual compromise to another danger.

"It is not for kings, O Lemuel, it is not for kings to drink wine; nor for princes strong drink: Lest they drink, and forget the law, and pervert the judgment of any of the afflicted." — Proverbs 31:4–5, KJV
Notice what frightens her.
She does not merely say that intoxication could embarrass the king.
She warns that it could cause him to forget the law and distort justice.
The Hebrew word shakhar (שָׁכַר) is associated with becoming drunk, while shekhar (שֵׁכָר) refers to an intoxicating drink.
Her concern is that a ruler entrusted with judgment must not surrender his discernment to intoxication.

This passage should not be twisted into a claim that every use of wine is universally condemned in Scripture. Other biblical passages distinguish wine from drunkenness, and Jesus Himself attended a wedding where He turned water into wine (John 2:1–11).
The warning here is specifically about the disastrous consequences of impaired judgment in someone responsible for others.
And that principle reaches far beyond alcohol.
What is clouding your judgment?
Maybe it is resentment.
Maybe it is greed.
Maybe it is an obsession with approval.
Maybe it is an addiction you keep minimizing because admitting its power would mean admitting your need for help.
Maybe you have become so intoxicated by ambition that you no longer recognize the people being hurt along the way.
You don't have to hold a glass to lose your moral clarity.
Pride can intoxicate.
Power can intoxicate.
Anger can intoxicate.
Even the applause of a crowd can make someone forget the truth they once promised to defend.
And this mother's concern is painfully practical.
When a leader loses self-control, other people pay the price.
The neglected child.
The betrayed spouse.
The employee who cannot defend himself.
The family waiting for justice.
The person whose suffering is dismissed because the powerful have become too distracted to care.
But then the passage takes a turn that many readers find confusing.
"Give strong drink unto him that is ready to perish, and wine unto those that be of heavy hearts. Let him drink, and forget his poverty, and remember his misery no more." — Proverbs 31:6–7, KJV
Is this mother suddenly encouraging drunkenness?
No responsible reading should isolate these words from their context.
The verses contrast the king's duty to remain clearheaded with the ancient use of intoxicating drink as relief for people experiencing extreme suffering or approaching death.

Interpreters differ over whether the words are primarily compassionate counsel, proverbial contrast, or an element of irony. They do not provide a sound basis for prescribing alcohol as a modern treatment for poverty, grief, or emotional distress.
The passage is not a license to abandon suffering people to intoxication.
The larger argument is that the king must preserve his judgment because vulnerable people need him to act justly.
And this leads to the mother's most extraordinary command.
"Open thy mouth for the dumb in the cause of all such as are appointed to destruction. Open thy mouth, judge righteously, and plead the cause of the poor and needy." — Proverbs 31:8–9, KJV
There it is.
The destination of her warning.
She did not simply want her son to avoid scandal.
She wanted him to defend people who could not defend themselves.
The Hebrew command is unforgettable.
פְּתַח־פִּיךָ
Petach-pikha.
"Open your mouth."
And then again:
פְּתַח־פִּיךָ שְׁפָט־צֶדֶק
Petach-pikha, shefat-tsedeq.
"Open your mouth; judge righteously."
The word tsedeq (צֶדֶק) carries the sense of righteousness and justice.
This is not an invitation to perform goodness for public admiration.
It is a command to exercise authority with moral integrity.
The king must speak when silence would abandon the vulnerable.
He must judge fairly when favoritism would be easier.
He must recognize that the poor and needy are not disposable people at the edge of his kingdom.
They are human beings whose lives matter before God.
And suddenly the mother's three warnings become one unified message.
Do not waste your strength on destructive desire.
Do not surrender your judgment to intoxication.
Do not use your authority for yourself while forgetting those who need protection.
She is teaching her son that leadership is stewardship.
That influence is responsibility.
That greatness without righteousness is a dangerous illusion.
And now the question turns toward us.
When was the last time you used your voice for someone who had none?
When did you last defend someone who could not repay you?
When did you choose truth even though silence would have protected your comfort?
It is possible to be loud about religion and strangely silent about injustice.
Possible to argue over doctrine while treating vulnerable people without compassion.
Possible to defend your reputation more passionately than you defend the truth.
Possible to know the right verses and still refuse the costly obedience those verses demand.
And before we point toward corrupt kings, we must examine the smaller kingdoms we have built around ourselves.
Our homes.
Our workplaces.
Our businesses.
Our ministries.
Our relationships.
Our online communities.
The people affected by our decisions.
The people who trust us to be fair.
The people who are afraid to speak because we hold more influence than they do.
The mother of Lemuel confronts every one of those kingdoms.
She reminds us that the question is not merely whether we possess power.
The question is what happens to other people when we exercise it.
And here is where the Gospel brings this ancient passage into even sharper focus.
Because when we read about the kind of king Lemuel was called to become, we eventually have to ask:
Has any human king fulfilled this calling perfectly?
Solomon did not.
David did not.
The history of Israel's monarchy repeatedly shows rulers who failed through pride, injustice, idolatry, violence, and unfaithfulness.
Even the most celebrated kings were imperfect men.
And we are not fundamentally different.
We have misused our strength.
We have made selfish choices.
We have allowed fear to silence us.
We have ignored suffering when responding would have cost us something.
We have chosen what was easy over what was righteous.
The mother's commands expose a standard we cannot claim to have fulfilled perfectly.
But Scripture does not leave us staring hopelessly at our failures.
It points us toward a greater King.
Jesus Christ.
The King who was not corrupted by temptation.
The King who did not exploit the vulnerable.
The King who refused to exchange obedience to the Father for the kingdoms of this world.
When Satan offered Him worldly authority in exchange for worship, Jesus refused (Matthew 4:8–10).
When religious leaders used power to burden others, Jesus confronted their hypocrisy.
When society pushed suffering people aside, Jesus drew near.
He touched lepers.
He welcomed children.
He showed mercy to sinners.
He proclaimed good news to the poor.
And when He stood before Pontius Pilate, the contrast between worldly power and divine kingship became breathtaking.
Pilate possessed the machinery of Roman authority.
Jesus stood before him accused, rejected, and approaching crucifixion.
Yet the One standing in apparent weakness was the true King.
Jesus declared:
"My kingdom is not of this world." — John 18:36, KJV
His kingship was not founded upon the coercive methods of fallen earthly kingdoms.
And the King who had every right to be served had already taught His disciples something revolutionary.
"For even the Son of man came not to be ministered unto, but to minister, and to give his life a ransom for many." — Mark 10:45, KJV
Read that again.
He came to serve.
And to give His life.
The mother of Lemuel wanted a king who would use his strength for others.
In Jesus Christ, we behold the King who gave Himself for sinners.
She warned against a king whose desires would destroy his people.
Jesus obeyed the Father even when obedience led to the cross.
She warned against a king whose judgment would be corrupted.
Jesus is the righteous Judge who cannot be bribed, manipulated, or deceived.
She commanded her son to speak for those without a voice.
Jesus is the risen Lord who intercedes for His people (Romans 8:34).
And here is the beautiful distinction we must never miss.
Jesus did not come merely to provide a better example of moral leadership.
He came to save sinners.
Including people who have failed every warning in this passage.
People whose desires have damaged relationships.
People whose addictions have harmed families.
People who remained silent when they should have defended someone.
People who abused influence.
People who carry memories they wish they could erase.
People who believe their scandal has permanently disqualified them from grace.
Perhaps that person is you.
Perhaps nobody knows the whole story.
They see your smile, but not your regret.
They hear your prayers, but not the accusations that rise inside your mind when the room becomes quiet.
They see your Sunday appearance, but not the struggle that follows you home.
You know what you did.
You know what you allowed.
You know the opportunities you wasted and the people you disappointed.
And sometimes you wonder whether God still wants anything to do with someone who knew better and still chose wrongly.
Listen carefully.
The cross of Jesus Christ is not proof that sin is insignificant.
It is proof that sin is so serious that our redemption required the sacrifice of the Son of God.
And it is also proof that God's mercy is greater than the hopelessness of a repentant sinner.
"If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness." — 1 John 1:9, KJV
That is not permission to continue hiding.
It is an invitation to come into the light.
Grace does not tell an unfaithful person to keep betraying.
Grace calls that person to repentance and faithfulness.
Grace does not tell an unjust leader to preserve appearances.
Grace calls that leader to righteousness, accountability, and, where possible, restitution.
Grace does not tell the addicted person that destructive bondage is harmless.
Grace invites surrender, truth, and the practical help necessary for recovery.
And grace does not promise that earthly consequences will instantly disappear.
Forgiveness is real.
Restoration is possible.
But repentance must never be confused with escaping responsibility.
The Jesus who forgives also transforms.
And sometimes His transforming work begins with the painful courage to admit:
"Lord, I have not been who You called me to be."
That confession can feel like the end of everything.
But in Christ, it can become the beginning of a different life.
It is not the claim that Jesus erases historical facts or pretends evil never happened.
It is the proclamation that through His death and resurrection, Jesus can redeem sinners, break the dominion of sin, and create a new direction where rebellion once ruled.
"Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new." — 2 Corinthians 5:17, KJV
The person who once exploited others can learn to serve.
The person who once lived for appetite can learn self-control through the Spirit.
The person who once stayed silent can begin speaking truth.
The person who once used influence selfishly can begin using it for the good of others.
Not because human effort can purchase salvation.
But because the grace that saves us also teaches us to live differently (Titus 2:11–12).
And maybe that is what someone reading this desperately needs to hear tonight.
You are not beyond the reach of Christ's mercy.
But you cannot cling to the very darkness from which He is calling you.
There is a difference between being ashamed of being caught and being brokenhearted over sin.
There is a difference between wanting consequences to disappear and wanting your heart to change.
There is a difference between looking religious and surrendering to Jesus.
The King who died for sinners is worthy of more than our carefully managed appearances.
He is worthy of our repentance.
Our trust.
Our obedience.
Our lives.
And if this message has exposed something you have been hiding, you do not need to manufacture a dramatic public confession to prove your sincerity.
Start by being truthful before God.
Seek forgiveness where you have sinned.
Make amends where appropriate and possible.
Ask for help where you are trapped.
And remember that genuine repentance bears fruit over time.
Not as a performance of holiness.
But as an honest testimony that you do not want to surrender your life to the darkness.
And if your struggle is too private to share publicly, bring it before the Lord and speak with a trustworthy pastor or mature believer who can walk with you.
Because Christian community should be a place where truth and compassion meet.
Not a stage where wounded people are pressured to expose every scar.
Now return, for one final moment, to that mother speaking to her son.
Imagine her looking into his eyes.
She knows she cannot follow him into every room.
She cannot make every decision for him.
She cannot force wisdom into his heart.
All she can do is tell him the truth and entrust him to the responsibility that comes with it.
And what does she choose to emphasize?
Not how to become richer.
Not how to become more famous.
Not how to defeat every rival.
She tells him to guard his strength.
Preserve his judgment.
And open his mouth for those who cannot speak for themselves.
What an extraordinary picture of love.
A mother who loved her son enough to warn him about becoming the kind of man who would harm others.
Perhaps you are a parent reading this, worried about a child who seems to be drifting away from God.
You have prayed.
You have spoken.
You have cried in private.
And sometimes you wonder whether any of your words are reaching them.
Proverbs 31:1–9 does not guarantee that every child will obey a godly parent's instruction.
But it reminds us that faithful words matter, even when we cannot control the outcome.
Speak truth with love.
Model the character you are teaching.
Pray without pretending you possess the power to change another person's heart.
And entrust the results to the Lord.
Perhaps you are the son or daughter who needs to remember the warnings you once dismissed.
Maybe someone loved you enough to tell you that your choices were leading toward destruction.
At the time, you called it interference.
Now you recognize it as concern.
If that person is still alive, perhaps today is the day to thank them.
Or perhaps you are a leader who needs to examine how your decisions affect people with less power than you.
Are you fair when nobody can challenge you?
Do you listen to the poor as attentively as you listen to the influential?
Do you use Scripture to serve people, or do you sometimes use religious language to shield yourself from accountability?
Would those closest to you describe your leadership as compassionate and truthful?
These are not comfortable questions.
But the Word of God was never given merely to make us comfortable.
It was given to make us wise, to reveal our sin, and to direct us toward the Lord.
And this is where the message of Proverbs 31 becomes deeply personal for Gospel Warrior.
We do not share Scripture merely to create religious content.
Our desire is to help people encounter biblical truth, understand the Gospel, and grow in genuine discipleship.
We want the exhausted believer to find encouragement in Christ.
The confused seeker to hear the truth about Jesus.
The struggling Christian to discover that repentance and grace belong together.
The wounded person to find compassionate, Scripture-grounded support.
And the spiritually complacent person to be awakened by the seriousness and beauty of following the Lord.
That is why sharing this article can matter.
Somewhere on your Facebook friends list may be a father whose private choices are damaging his family.
A mother praying for her son.
A young person being drawn toward destructive relationships.
A Christian leader struggling with compromise.
Someone who thinks Jesus would never receive them after what they have done.
You cannot know what God may do through a faithful witness.
But you can make the message available.
Not because following a page makes anyone a Christian.
But because the truths we allow into our daily lives can help shape what we remember, meditate upon, and obey.
We also want to invite you into something deeper than occasionally encountering an article.
These resources are intended to help believers go beyond inspirational moments into sustained study, prayer, spiritual maturity, and faithful living.
If you have been praying for a way to use part of what God has entrusted to you for Gospel-centered work, this is one opportunity to consider.
But we also want to be biblically clear.
Scripture teaches believers to give willingly, thoughtfully, and cheerfully, not through guilt or compulsion (2 Corinthians 9:7).
You glorify God first and foremost through faith in Jesus Christ and a life offered to Him in obedience, love, truth, and worship.
Supporting sound biblical ministry can be one expression of that stewardship.
The heart of this invitation is not merchandise.
It is helping biblical truth reach people who need it.
It is supporting a community committed to pointing people away from spiritual performance and toward Jesus Christ.
Because the message of salvation cannot be bought.
Jesus has already paid the price for the redemption of His people.
And that brings us back to the most important question in this entire passage.
What was Lemuel's mother really trying to protect?
His reputation?
Yes, perhaps in part.
His kingdom?
Certainly, his decisions would affect it.
His people?
Absolutely. Their welfare was at the center of her commands.
But beneath all of that was something more fundamental.
She was teaching him not to surrender his God-given responsibilities to his appetites.
She wanted him to remain the kind of man who could recognize righteousness and act upon it.
She wanted his strength to serve something greater than himself.
And that is still the calling confronting us today.
What are you doing with the strength God has entrusted to you?
What is ruling your heart?
Who suffers when you compromise?
Who benefits when you obey?
And above all, have you surrendered yourself to the one King who is perfectly righteous?
Because Proverbs 31:1–9 is not ultimately an invitation to congratulate ourselves for being better than corrupt rulers.
It is a summons to recognize our need for wisdom, righteousness, repentance, and the saving grace of Jesus Christ.
Maybe your life has been marked by scandal.
Maybe you are carrying regret.
Maybe you have wasted years chasing something that promised fulfillment but left your soul exhausted.
The call of Christ is not to pretend those years never happened.
It is to turn to Him.
To trust the Savior who died for sinners and rose again.
To receive His forgiveness through faith.
And to walk, by His grace, in the newness of life He gives.
Before you leave, I want to ask you something more important than whether you enjoyed this article.
What is one area of your life where you need Jesus to restore your judgment, purify your desires, or give you courage to do what is right?
If all you can say is "Christ is still healing me," that is enough.
Not to shame them.
Not to accuse them.
But to remind them that the door of repentance and mercy is open through Jesus Christ.
A mother once warned her son that a crown could not protect him from the destruction of an undisciplined heart.
And centuries later, the Gospel reveals a King who wore a crown of thorns to redeem people whose hearts had wandered far from God.
One mother pleaded with her son not to waste his strength.
The Son of God willingly laid down His life to save sinners.
And because He rose again, failure does not have to be the final word for those who turn to Him in faith.
The most tragic thing is not that you once fell into darkness—it is to hear the voice of the Savior calling you into the light and still refuse His hand.
